1 Kings 1.audience: Kings was written for a people who had lived under David's line for centuries. Readers would see here how Solomon, not the older Adonijah, came to the throne.

culture.title: Warming an old king
culture.text: A young woman, Abishag, is brought to care for the aged David and lie beside him for warmth. The text notes that the king "knew her not."

culture.title: Riding the king's mule
culture.text: Solomon rides David's own mule to Gihon to be anointed. Riding the king's animal publicly showed that David had chosen him.

culture.title: Holding the horns of the altar
culture.text: Adonijah grasps the horns of the altar to seek sanctuary. A person at the altar was under God's protection, although the law did not protect a deliberate murderer there (Exodus 21:14).

1 Kings 2.audience: Readers knew Joab, Abiathar, and Shimei from the stories of David. This chapter tells how each was dealt with as Solomon secured his throne.

culture.title: A king's last charge
culture.text: David's final words urge Solomon to keep the law of Moses, then turn to unfinished matters of loyalty and justice. Deathbed instructions to a successor were a recognized custom.

culture.title: Asking for the king's servant
culture.text: Adonijah asks to marry Abishag, who had served David. Solomon treats the request as a claim to the throne, as taking a king's woman could signify (2 Samuel 16:21–22).

culture.title: Confined to Jerusalem
culture.text: Shimei is ordered to live in Jerusalem and never cross the brook Kidron—a form of house arrest.

1 Kings 3.audience: Gibeon was the site of the tabernacle and its bronze altar in Solomon's day (2 Chronicles 1:3–6). Readers knew Solomon above all for the wisdom he asks for here.

culture.title: A marriage alliance with Egypt
culture.text: Solomon marries Pharaoh's daughter. Marriages between royal houses sealed alliances; an Egyptian princess given to a foreign king was a sign of the alliance's importance.

culture.title: Worship at high places
culture.text: Before the temple was built, the people sacrificed at local high places. The text notes this as the situation "because there was no house built unto the name of the LORD."

culture.title: The king as judge
culture.text: Kings heard cases directly, even from the poorest. Two prostitutes bring their dispute to Solomon himself.

1 Kings 4.audience: Readers would recognize this list of officials and districts as the administration of a kingdom at its height, with Israel and Judah "many, as the sand which is by the sea" (1 Kings 4:20).

culture.title: Twelve districts
culture.text: Solomon divided the land into twelve districts, each supplying the royal household for one month of the year. The districts do not all follow the old tribal borders.

culture.title: Feeding the court
culture.text: The daily provisions of the court—thirty measures of fine flour, sixty of meal, thirty oxen, a hundred sheep, and game—show the size of the royal household.

culture.title: Proverbs and songs
culture.text: Solomon spoke three thousand proverbs and a thousand and five songs, including sayings about trees, animals, birds, and fish. Collections of proverbs were a known form of wisdom in Egypt and Mesopotamia.

1 Kings 5.audience: Tyre was a wealthy Phoenician port to the north. Readers knew Hiram of Tyre as a friend of David and a partner in Solomon's building.

culture.title: Timber floated by sea
culture.text: Cedar and fir from Lebanon were brought down to the sea and floated in rafts along the coast, then hauled inland.

culture.title: Forced labor
culture.text: Solomon raises a levy of thirty thousand men, sending them to Lebanon in shifts of ten thousand, one month on and two months home.

culture.title: Cut stone
culture.text: Large, costly stones were quarried and dressed for the temple foundation. Fine ashlar masonry (squared stone) is known from royal buildings of this period.

1 Kings 6.audience: Readers knew this temple as the center of their worship for nearly four hundred years, until Babylon destroyed it (2 Kings 25:9). The chapter dates its building to 480 years after the exodus (1 Kings 6:1).

culture.title: The temple plan
culture.text: The temple had a porch, a main hall (the holy place), and an inner room (the oracle, or most holy place). Temples with this three-part plan are known from Syria, such as the one excavated at Ain Dara.

culture.title: Silent construction
culture.text: The stones were finished at the quarry, so that no hammer, axe, or iron tool was heard at the temple site.

culture.title: Months by name
culture.text: The text uses old month names—Zif (the second month) and Bul (the eighth)—and records seven years of building.

1 Kings 7.audience: The palace complex described here—with its hall of judgment and the house of the forest of Lebanon—was where Judah's kings ruled. Readers knew the bronze sea and pillars from the temple courtyard.

culture.title: Jachin and Boaz
culture.text: Two great bronze pillars stood at the temple porch, named Jachin and Boaz. Free-standing pillars at temple entrances are known from other temples in the region.

culture.title: Casting bronze in clay
culture.text: The bronze work was cast in clay molds in the Jordan valley between Succoth and Zarthan, where suitable clay was found.

culture.title: The molten sea
culture.text: A huge bronze basin, ten cubits across and resting on twelve bronze oxen, held water for the priests' washing (2 Chronicles 4:6).

1 Kings 8.audience: Solomon's prayer looks ahead to Israelites in many situations—defeat, drought, famine, and captivity in a far land (1 Kings 8:46–50). Later readers in exile heard it as speaking to their own condition.

culture.title: The month Ethanim
culture.text: The temple is dedicated in Ethanim, the seventh month, at the time of the feast of tabernacles.

culture.title: Praying toward the temple
culture.text: Solomon asks God to hear prayers made toward this house. Daniel later prays toward Jerusalem from Babylon (Daniel 6:10).

culture.title: A great sacrifice
culture.text: The dedication sacrifices number 22,000 oxen and 120,000 sheep. The bronze altar was too small, so the middle of the court was used (1 Kings 8:64).

1 Kings 9.audience: Readers knew Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer as fortified cities (1 Kings 9:15). The chapter also lists the Canaanite peoples Solomon used for forced labor.

culture.title: Gate complexes
culture.text: Archaeologists have uncovered similar large city gates with six chambers at Hazor, Megiddo, and Gezer. Many date them to Solomon's time; the dating is debated.

culture.title: Cabul
culture.text: Hiram is displeased with the twenty towns in Galilee Solomon gives him and calls the region Cabul, which the KJV notes means ‘displeasing’ or ‘dirty.’

culture.title: Ships to Ophir
culture.text: Solomon builds ships at Eziongeber on the Red Sea, and Hiram's experienced sailors bring gold from Ophir. Ophir's location is unknown.

1 Kings 10.audience: Readers knew Solomon's age as Israel's golden era of wealth and fame. Jesus later referred to the queen of Sheba's visit (Matthew 12:42).

culture.title: Sheba
culture.text: Sheba was in southern Arabia (modern Yemen), a land of incense and spices. Camel caravans carried its frankincense and myrrh north along the trade routes.

culture.title: Hard questions
culture.text: Rulers tested each other's wisdom with riddles and difficult questions. The queen comes "to prove him with hard questions."

culture.title: Horses and chariots
culture.text: Solomon's merchants traded horses and chariots between Egypt and the kings of the Hittites and Syria. A chariot cost 600 shekels of silver and a horse 150.

1 Kings 11.audience: Readers knew the high places Solomon built for Chemosh and Molech on the hill east of Jerusalem; Josiah later destroyed them (2 Kings 23:13).

culture.title: Gods of foreign wives
culture.text: Solomon builds shrines for Ashtoreth of the Sidonians, Milcom (Molech) of the Ammonites, and Chemosh of Moab. Foreign wives at court continued to worship their own gods.

culture.title: A torn garment as a sign
culture.text: The prophet Ahijah tears his new garment into twelve pieces and gives ten to Jeroboam—an acted-out message that ten tribes would be his.

culture.title: Political refugees in Egypt
culture.text: Jeroboam flees to Shishak king of Egypt. Egypt sheltered rivals of Solomon, including Hadad of Edom (1 Kings 11:17–19).

1 Kings 12.audience: Readers lived with the result of this chapter: two kingdoms, Israel in the north and Judah in the south. The text says Israel rebelled against David's house "unto this day" (1 Kings 12:19).

culture.title: Elders and young men
culture.text: Rehoboam consults the old men who had served Solomon, then the young men raised with him, and follows the young men's harsh advice.

culture.title: Golden calves at Bethel and Dan
culture.text: Jeroboam sets up two golden calves at the southern and northern ends of his kingdom. In the region, gods were often pictured standing on bulls.

culture.title: A new feast date
culture.text: Jeroboam sets a feast in the eighth month, a month after the feast of tabernacles in Judah.

1 Kings 13.audience: Readers knew the altar at Bethel as the center of the northern kingdom's worship. The prophecy here names Josiah, who burned bones on that altar centuries later (2 Kings 23:15–16).

culture.title: Not eating in the place
culture.text: The man of God is commanded not to eat or drink at Bethel. Sharing a meal implied fellowship with one's host.

culture.title: Lion attacks
culture.text: Lions lived in the land in biblical times, especially in the thickets of the Jordan (Jeremiah 49:19). Travelers on lonely roads could be attacked.

1 Kings 14.audience: Readers knew Shishak's invasion of Judah from this chapter. An Egyptian inscription at Karnak, from Pharaoh Shoshenq I, lists towns he conquered in Israel and Judah.

culture.title: Gifts for a prophet
culture.text: Jeroboam's wife brings ten loaves, cakes, and a jar of honey when consulting Ahijah—a customary gift for a seer.

culture.title: Gold shields replaced with bronze
culture.text: Shishak carries off Solomon's gold shields, and Rehoboam replaces them with bronze ones.

culture.title: The book of the chronicles
culture.text: The writer refers readers to "the book of the chronicles of the kings of Israel," royal records that do not survive.

1 Kings 15.audience: From here the book alternates between the kings of Judah and Israel. Readers would see each king dated by the reign of the king in the other kingdom (1 Kings 15:1, 9, 25).

culture.title: The queen mother
culture.text: The king's mother held an official position at court. Asa removes his grandmother Maachah from it because she made an idol.

culture.title: Buying an alliance
culture.text: Asa sends temple and palace treasure to Benhadad of Syria to break his treaty with Israel—a common way to buy military help.

1 Kings 16.audience: Readers knew Samaria as the capital of the northern kingdom, founded by Omri (1 Kings 16:24). Assyrian records later called Israel ‘the house of Omri.’

culture.title: Buying a hill for a capital
culture.text: Omri buys the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver and builds a new capital on it. Excavations there have uncovered the royal quarter of the Israelite kings.

culture.title: Baal of Sidon
culture.text: Ahab marries Jezebel, daughter of the king of the Sidonians, and builds a temple and altar for Baal in Samaria.

culture.title: Seven days' reign
culture.text: Zimri reigns only seven days before burning the palace over himself.

1 Kings 17.audience: Baal was worshipped as the god of rain and storms. Readers would see Elijah announce a drought in the name of the LORD at the height of Baal worship in Israel.

culture.title: Brooks that dry up
culture.text: Many streams in the land flow only in the rainy season. Without rain, the brook Cherith dries up.

culture.title: Zarephath
culture.text: Zarephath was a Phoenician town between Tyre and Sidon—in Jezebel's home territory. Jesus mentions the widow there (Luke 4:25–26).

culture.title: A widow's last meal
culture.text: The widow has only a handful of flour in a barrel and a little oil in a jar—enough for one last meal. Widows were among the poorest in ancient society.

1 Kings 18.audience: Mount Carmel was a ridge overlooking the Mediterranean on the border with Phoenicia. Readers would see the contest there decide whether the LORD or Baal was God.

culture.title: Prophets of Baal and Asherah
culture.text: Jezebel supported 450 prophets of Baal and 400 prophets of the groves (Asherah) who ate at her table.

culture.title: Cutting themselves
culture.text: The prophets of Baal cut themselves with knives and lances, a practice Israel's law forbade (Leviticus 19:28; Deuteronomy 14:1). Texts from Ugarit describe self-cutting in mourning.

culture.title: A cloud from the sea
culture.text: Rain in the land comes from the west, off the Mediterranean. A small cloud rising from the sea signaled the coming storm.

1 Kings 19.audience: Horeb was the mountain of God where Moses received the law. Readers would see Elijah travel forty days and nights to the same mountain (1 Kings 19:8).

culture.title: A juniper tree
culture.text: The "juniper" is the broom tree, a desert shrub that gives some shade. Its roots were also burned for charcoal (Psalm 120:4).

culture.title: Plowing with twelve yoke
culture.text: Elisha is plowing with twelve yoke of oxen, a sign of a wealthy family. He sacrifices his oxen and burns the equipment, leaving his old life behind.

culture.title: The prophet's mantle
culture.text: Elijah throws his mantle (cloak) over Elisha, a sign of passing on his role. Elisha later takes up the mantle when Elijah is taken (2 Kings 2:13).

1 Kings 20.audience: Syria (Aram), with its capital at Damascus, was Israel's main rival to the northeast in Ahab's day.

culture.title: Kings in tents
culture.text: Benhadad and thirty-two allied kings are drinking in their pavilions at noon when Israel attacks.

culture.title: Gods of the hills
culture.text: Benhadad's servants say Israel's gods are "gods of the hills," so Syria should fight on the plain. Many ancient peoples believed gods ruled particular territories.

culture.title: Sackcloth and ropes
culture.text: Benhadad's servants come with sackcloth on their loins and ropes on their heads to beg for mercy, signs of complete submission.

1 Kings 21.audience: Israel's law kept family land within the family (Leviticus 25:23; Numbers 36:7). Readers would understand why Naboth refuses to sell his ancestral vineyard.

culture.title: The inheritance of my fathers
culture.text: Naboth says, "The LORD forbid it me, that I should give the inheritance of my fathers unto thee." He refuses even when Ahab offers a better vineyard or its worth in money (1 Kings 21:2).

culture.title: Letters with the king's seal
culture.text: Jezebel writes letters in Ahab's name and seals them with his seal, giving them royal authority.

culture.title: Two false witnesses
culture.text: Two witnesses were required for a death sentence (Deuteronomy 17:6). Jezebel arranges two false witnesses to accuse Naboth.

1 Kings 22.audience: Readers knew Ramoth-gilead as a city east of the Jordan, disputed between Israel and Syria. Jehoshaphat of Judah joins Ahab here—an alliance between the two kingdoms.

culture.title: Court prophets
culture.text: Kings consulted prophets before war. Ahab gathers about four hundred prophets, who all promise victory; Micaiah alone speaks differently.

culture.title: A disguised king
culture.text: Ahab disguises himself in battle, while Jehoshaphat wears his royal robes. The king of Syria orders his chariot captains to fight only with the king of Israel (1 Kings 22:31).

culture.title: Ivory house
culture.text: Ahab built "the ivory house." Carved ivory panels used to decorate furniture and walls have been found at Samaria.
